Q1.text: The goal is to build a foundation model for image segmentation that can be prompted, similar to how language models are prompted, and that generalizes zero-shot to new data distributions and tasks.
The paper frames the problem as three entangled questions: what task enables zero-shot generalization, what model architecture fits it, and what data can power it.

Q2.text: Foundation models pre-trained on web-scale data have driven strong zero-shot and few-shot generalization in NLP and, to a lesser extent, in computer vision through image-text models such as CLIP and ALIGN.
Computer vision includes many problems beyond vision-language encoders, segmentation among them, for which abundant training data does not exist.

Q3.text: There is no web-scale data source for segmentation masks, unlike the web-scale text and image-text corpora that power other foundation models.

Prior multi-task segmentation systems perform a fixed set of tasks where training and test tasks are the same, unlike a model that can perform new tasks at inference time via prompting and composition.

Q4.text: The authors introduce a promptable segmentation task, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with an image encoder, prompt encoder, and mask decoder, and a data engine used to collect the SA-1B dataset.
SAM predicts multiple (by default 3) candidate masks per prompt along with a predicted IoU confidence score for each, to handle prompt ambiguity.

The data engine has three stages (assisted-manual, semi-automatic, fully automatic); the fully automatic stage, prompting SAM with a 32x32 point grid, produced the 1.1B masks on 11M images that make up SA-1B.
Given a precomputed image embedding, the prompt encoder and mask decoder predict a mask in about 50 milliseconds in a web browser on CPU.

Q5.text: The model separates a heavyweight image encoder (run once per image) from a lightweight prompt encoder and mask decoder so the image embedding cost can be amortized across many different prompts.
SAM predicts multiple masks per prompt because with a single output the model averages multiple valid masks when a prompt (e.g., a point on a shirt) could refer to more than one object.
The authors chose an MAE-pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT-H/16) image encoder, motivated by scalability and access to strong pretraining.

Q6.text: The paper reports five zero-shot transfer experiments: single-point valid mask evaluation on 23 datasets, edge detection on BSDS500, object proposal generation on LVIS, instance segmentation on COCO/LVIS, and a text-to-mask proof-of-concept.
The paper also runs a Responsible AI fairness analysis measuring SAM's person-segmentation performance across perceived gender presentation, age group, and skin tone.
Ablation experiments vary the data-engine training stage, the amount of SA-1B training data (0.1M/1M/11M images), and the image encoder size (ViT-B/L/H).

Q7.text: From a single center point, SAM produces higher mIoU than the RITM baseline on 16 of 23 datasets, by as much as about 47 IoU; with an oracle picking the best of its 3 masks, SAM outperforms RITM on all 23 datasets.
On BSDS500 zero-shot edge detection, SAM scores ODS .768, OIS .786, AP .794, R50 .928, compared to the learned HED baseline's ODS .788, OIS .808, AP .840, R50 .923.
On LVIS v1 instance segmentation, SAM prompted with ViTDet-H boxes achieves mask AP 44.7 versus the fully-supervised ViTDet-H's 46.6; on COCO, SAM achieves AP 46.5 versus ViTDet-H's 51.0.
In a human 1-10 mask-quality rating study on LVIS (both models prompted with LVIS ground-truth boxes), SAM's masks averaged 8.1 versus ViTDet-H's 7.9, despite SAM's lower AP.

Q8.text: The results establish that SAM's zero-shot single-point segmentation is competitive with, and on most datasets better than, the strongest prior interactive segmentation baseline (RITM) across a diverse 23-dataset suite.

On a 500-image (~50k-mask) sample, 94% of automatic masks had over 90% IoU with their professionally corrected versions (97% over 75% IoU), which the authors set alongside prior inter-annotator consistency estimates of 85-91% IoU.

The results establish that SAM can be composed with an existing object detector (ViTDet) to perform zero-shot instance segmentation, trailing the fully-supervised specialist in mask AP but reasonably close to it.
The fairness analysis finds that within each of the gender, age, and skin-tone groupings, SAM's person-segmentation confidence intervals overlap, except older vs. middle age.

Q9.text: The results do not establish a quantitative measure of the text-to-mask capability; it is presented only as a qualitative proof-of-concept that the authors call exploratory and not entirely robust.

The fairness results do not rule out bias in downstream use: the authors acknowledge biases may arise when SAM is used as a component in larger systems and recommend users run their own fairness evaluations.
For clothing segmentation, SAM shows a bias across perceived gender presentation with a one-point prompt (masculine 81.0 vs. feminine 76.3 mIoU, disjoint 95% intervals); the gap closes at 3 points.
The paper does not establish that SAM achieves the status of a foundation model; the authors say this remains to be seen by how it is used in the community.

Q10.text: The authors state their principal contributions are a new task (promptable segmentation), a new model (SAM), and a new dataset (SA-1B) intended to lift image segmentation into the era of foundation models.

Q11.text: SAM can miss fine structures, occasionally hallucinates small disconnected components, and does not produce boundaries as crisp as more computationally intensive zoom-in methods.
Dedicated interactive segmentation methods are expected to outperform SAM when many points are provided, since SAM is designed for generality rather than high-IoU interactive segmentation.
SAM's overall performance is not real-time when using a heavy image encoder, even though prompts are processed in real time.
It is unclear how to design simple prompts that implement semantic and panoptic segmentation with SAM.

Q12.text: Segment Anything introduces a promptable segmentation task, the SAM model, and the SA-1B dataset of 1.1 billion masks on 11 million images, aiming to bring foundation-model-style prompting to segmentation.

SAM's zero-shot performance is often competitive with or superior to prior fully supervised results, though it trails fully-supervised specialists on some benchmark metrics such as instance-segmentation mask AP.
Given a precomputed image embedding, SAM produces a mask from a prompt in about 50 milliseconds, enabling real-time interactive use in a browser.
